tagline: The story of the first exiles to come home from Babylon, the rebuilding of God's temple under Persian rule, and a scribe who called a small, battered people back to the law of Moses.
overview:
Ezra begins where the books of Kings and Chronicles leave off: Jerusalem is in ruins, its temple burned, and the people of Judah scattered in Babylon. Then, in 539 BC, the Persian king Cyrus conquers Babylon, and the next year he allows the exiles to go home and rebuild the house of their God. The first half of the book (chapters 1 to 6) tells how the first returnees, led by Zerubbabel, a descendant of King David, and Jeshua the high priest, set up the altar, lay the temple's foundation, meet years of local opposition, and finally finish the building in 515 BC, prodded by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah.

The second half (chapters 7 to 10) jumps ahead nearly sixty years. Ezra, a priest and a scribe trained in the law of Moses, leads a second group from Babylon to Jerusalem with the backing of King Artaxerxes. He finds that many of the returned exiles, including priests and leaders, have married women from the surrounding peoples, and the book ends with a painful public reckoning over those marriages.

Ezra is a book about what it means to be God's people after the catastrophe. There is no king on David's throne, no independence, and no miracle on the scale of the exodus. There are imperial decrees, building permits, genealogies, and a great deal of paperwork. The book's claim is that God is at work in exactly those things: stirring the heart of a foreign emperor, keeping his promises through prophets, and rebuilding a people around worship and the word of God. It is a small beginning, and the book knows it, but it is a real one.
author:
The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Babylonian Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a), holds that Ezra wrote his own book, and parts of it are plainly his: chapters 7:27 to 9:15 are written in the first person, as Ezra's own memoir. Other parts speak of Ezra in the third person, and the book also contains lists of returnees and official letters in Aramaic, which point to a compiler who gathered and arranged sources.

For much of the modern period scholars treated Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles as one work by a single writer or school, often called the Chronicler, pointing to shared interests (the temple, the Levites, genealogies) and to the fact that the last verses of 2 Chronicles repeat the first verses of Ezra. Since the 1960s and 1970s, scholars such as Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson have argued on linguistic and theological grounds that Ezra-Nehemiah is a separate work from Chronicles, and many now hold that view. Others still see a close relationship. What is not in doubt is that Ezra and Nehemiah were counted as a single book in the Hebrew tradition; the division into two books appears first in Christian tradition and entered Hebrew manuscripts and printed Hebrew Bibles only in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
date:
The events of the book run from Cyrus's decree in 539/538 BC to the marriage reform that follows Ezra's arrival. That arrival is dated to the seventh year of King Artaxerxes (7:7). If this is Artaxerxes I, which is the traditional view and still the most widely held, Ezra came to Jerusalem in 458 BC, thirteen years before Nehemiah. Some scholars argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, which would place Ezra in 398 BC, after Nehemiah; a smaller group proposes reading the thirty-seventh year of Artaxerxes I, about 428 BC. The arguments turn on details such as which high priest was in office and how Ezra and Nehemiah relate in Nehemiah 8 and 12, where they appear together.

The finished book of Ezra-Nehemiah was probably put together in the late fifth or fourth century BC. Its lists of priests reach to a Jaddua and a Johanan (Nehemiah 12:11, 22), which suggests a date no earlier than about 400 BC for the final form.
setting:
Ezra is set in the Persian Empire, the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from Egypt and Asia Minor to the borders of India. The Persians ruled through provinces called satrapies. Judah, now a small province called Yehud, sat inside the great satrapy the Persians called Beyond the River, meaning the lands west of the Euphrates. Its official language was Aramaic, which is why parts of Ezra (4:8 to 6:18 and 7:12-26) are written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.

The Persian kings in the book are Cyrus (who took Babylon in 539 BC), Darius I (522-486 BC), Xerxes (486-465 BC), and Artaxerxes I (465-424 BC). Persian policy generally allowed subject peoples to keep their own gods and temples, and sometimes paid for them, in return for loyalty and taxes. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder now in the British Museum, records Cyrus returning displaced gods and peoples to their homes in Mesopotamia. It does not mention the Jews, but it fits the kind of decree Ezra 1 describes. The returning exiles found a small, poor Judah, surrounded by neighbors in Samaria, Ammon, and elsewhere who had their own claims on the land and their own reasons to resent the newcomers.
purpose: The book was written for the Jewish community in and around Jerusalem after the exile, a people who had come home to a land they did not control and a temple far humbler than Solomon's. It answers their questions. Are we still God's people? Did his promises survive the exile? How should we live now, with no king and a foreign empire over us? Ezra's answer is that God has kept his word through Jeremiah, that the rebuilt temple is truly his house, and that the community's life must now be ordered by the law of Moses. The book also warns: the return from exile does not by itself cure the unfaithfulness that caused the exile, and the community must guard its distinct life with God.
story: Ezra picks up the Bible's story at its lowest point. Second Kings ends with the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC and the exile to Babylon, and Second Chronicles ends with Cyrus's decree, the same words that open Ezra. Ezra tells the first chapters of the return, and Nehemiah continues the account with the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls about 445 BC. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah belong to the years of Ezra 5 and 6, and Malachi probably speaks to the same community some decades later. Esther tells a story of Jews who stayed in Persia during the same era. After Ezra-Nehemiah, the Old Testament's narrative falls silent, and the next chapter of the story opens with the Gospels, some four centuries later, in a Judea under Rome with a temple descended from the one finished in Ezra 6.
christ: Ezra is a book of partial fulfillments. The exiles come home, but they remain subjects of a foreign king. A son of David, Zerubbabel, leads them, but he is a governor, not a king. The temple is rebuilt, but the old men weep because it is so much less than the first (3:12), and nowhere does the book say that God's glory fills it, as it filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple. The prophets of the period, Haggai and Zechariah, look beyond this modest house to a greater glory and a coming king. The New Testament hears those longings answered in Jesus. Matthew's genealogy runs through Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12-13), John says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and Jesus speaks of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21). The return under Cyrus is a real act of God's faithfulness, and it is also a signpost toward a deeper return from exile that the book itself does not reach.
reading: Ezra is history written by a believing community, built from sources: lists, royal letters, and Ezra's own memoir. Read it with the documents in mind, and don't skip the lists, which are the book's way of saying that every family and every returnee counted. Watch for the refrain about the hand of God being on Ezra (7:6, 7:28, 8:18, 8:31), which is how the book sees God at work through ordinary events. Notice that the book is not strictly chronological: 4:6-23 jumps forward to later kings to show a pattern of opposition, then 4:24 returns to the reign of Darius. Finally, read chapters 9 and 10 carefully and in context. They are not about ethnicity in the modern sense but about faithfulness to the covenant, and they raise real moral questions that later Scripture, including the book of Ruth, helps a reader think through.

structure.title: The return under Cyrus
structure.summary: Cyrus decrees that the temple be rebuilt and returns its sacred vessels. The first exiles go home, and the book lists them family by family.

structure.title: The temple rebuilt
structure.summary: The returnees set up the altar and lay the foundation, meet opposition that halts the work for years, then resume under the prophets Haggai and Zechariah and finish the temple in the sixth year of Darius, 515 BC.

structure.title: Ezra comes to Jerusalem
structure.summary: Almost sixty years later Ezra the scribe leads a second group from Babylon with a commission from Artaxerxes to teach and apply the law of God, and arrives safely with the temple's gifts.

structure.title: The crisis of the mixed marriages
structure.summary: Ezra learns that many have married women of the surrounding peoples, prays a great prayer of confession, and leads the community in a painful covenant to separate from those marriages.

themes.title: God works through empires
themes.body: Ezra opens with God stirring the spirit of a Persian king, and it keeps returning to royal decrees, letters, and archives. The book's conviction is that the God of heaven rules the kings of the earth, turning their hearts and using their policies to keep his promises to a small people. This is providence without spectacle: no sea parts, but the paperwork comes through.

themes.title: Worship at the center
themes.body: The first thing the returnees build is an altar, and the first great project is the temple. The book lingers over sacrifices, feasts, Levites, singers, and the Passover. The community is being rebuilt around the presence and worship of God, and its identity comes from gathering there rather than from a king or a territory.

themes.title: The word of God rules the community
themes.body: Again and again things are done as it is written in the law of Moses. Ezra himself is introduced as a scribe who studied, practiced, and taught that law (7:10). The book marks a turn in Israel's history toward Scripture as the center of common life, a turn that shaped Judaism and the world into which Jesus was born.

themes.title: A remnant and its faithfulness
themes.body: The returnees see themselves as a remnant, the survivors God has spared. That brings gratitude and also fear, because the sins that caused the exile could return. Ezra's prayer in chapter 9 is a model of corporate confession in which the leader counts himself among the guilty.

themes.title: Opposition and perseverance
themes.body: From chapter 4 onward, every step of rebuilding meets resistance: offers of help with strings attached, discouragement, accusations to the king, forced stoppages. The book is honest that faithful work can stall for years and that God's timing includes long delays.

keyChapters.why: Cyrus's decree fulfills the word spoken through Jeremiah and begins the return from exile, told with echoes of the first exodus.
The altar is rebuilt and the foundation laid, and joy and weeping rise together as the old men remember Solomon's temple.
Darius confirms Cyrus's decree, the temple is finished and dedicated in 515 BC, and the returned exiles keep the Passover.
Ezra is introduced as a scribe devoted to studying, practicing, and teaching the law, and Artaxerxes commissions him.
Ezra's prayer of confession, in which the leader stands with his guilty people, is one of the great prayers of the Old Testament.
